design_detail: Systematic review and DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis of 84 prospective cohort publications (Medline and Embase to September 2009) comparing people who drank at baseline with non-drinkers for five cardiovascular outcomes: cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, incident coronary heart disease (CHD), CHD mortality, incident stroke and stroke mortality. All-cause mortality was pooled as a secondary outcome from the 31 included studies that happened to report it. The main contrast is any current drinking against non-drinking, a reference group that in most cohorts included former drinkers; intake categories in g/day, sex, a lifetime-abstainer reference, former drinkers, the number of covariates and the length of follow-up were examined in stratified analyses. Not registered; reported to MOOSE. The companion review of interventional biomarker studies on which the causal argument leans (Brien et al., BMJ 2011;342:d636) was not read.
can_establish: The average association, in prospective cohorts published up to September 2009, between drinking at baseline and later cardiovascular events compared with not drinking, and how that association differs by intake category, sex, choice of reference group, extent of confounder adjustment and length of follow-up.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking lowers cardiovascular risk (observational cohorts, with residual confounding and with former and occasional drinkers in the reference group only partly examined); the shape of the dose–response relation (each intake category pooled separately from the studies that reported it, without a dose–response model); effects of drinking pattern or beverage (not analysed); and all-cause mortality as a systematic finding (the all-cause estimate comes only from cardiovascular studies that also reported it).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Medline 1950 to September 2009; Embase 1980 to September 2009) without language restriction, plus bibliographies of identified articles and reviews, proceedings of three cardiology meetings (2007–2009) and contact with experts about missed, ongoing or unpublished studies; published and unpublished studies were eligible (Methods › Data sources and searches, 1st paragraph; Study selection, 2nd paragraph). The pooled cohorts are general-population, occupational and health-professional cohorts (Table 1: for example the Physicians' Health Study, Nurses' Health Study, Framingham, Kaiser Permanente, Cancer Prevention Study II) from the USA, Europe, Japan, China, Australia and Canada. Pooled participants per outcome range from 458,811 (incident stroke) to 1,925,106 (CHD mortality) (Table 2, column headers).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: prospective cohort studies of adults aged 18 or over without pre-existing cardiovascular disease, comparing current alcohol use with non-drinkers, reporting CVD mortality, incident CHD (fatal or non-fatal incident myocardial infarction, angina, ischaemic heart disease or coronary revascularisation), CHD mortality, incident stroke (ischaemic or haemorrhagic) or stroke mortality; authors were contacted when a cohort's risk profile was unclear. Excluded: outcomes predefined as ineligible (for example chronic congestive heart failure or stable angina), non-atherothrombotic end points such as arrhythmias, composite end points, non-cardiovascular outcomes and duplicate reports (Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph; Results › Identification of studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Of the 84 publications, 34 (40%) studied all-male cohorts, 6 (7%) women only and 44 (52%) both sexes (Results › Identification of studies). Table 1 gives cohort, size (286 to 581,321), country, percentage of men, age range and follow-up (2.5 to 35 years; mean 11, SD 6). Several cohorts contribute more than one publication, usually to different outcomes (the Physicians' Health Study four times; the Nurses' Health Study, Framingham, Kaiser Permanente and the Copenhagen City Heart Study three times each).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; loss to follow-up within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The review pools whatever comparison each cohort reported: in most, the non-drinker reference group mixed lifetime abstainers with former drinkers, some of whom may have stopped because of illness; only 7 to 9 studies per outcome (3 for stroke mortality) used lifetime abstainers (Table 2). Cohorts are mostly from high-income countries, 40% are all-male, and several are occupational or health-professional groups (physicians, nurses, petroleum-industry workers, health professionals). Two databases only, supplemented by hand-searching, proceedings and expert contact. Two Table 1 entries do not fit the stated criteria, and some cohorts may contribute overlapping participants to the same pool (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported alcohol intake at each cohort's baseline, as reported by the primary studies. The reviewers expressed intake in grams of ethanol per day, assuming 12.5 g per drink where a study did not state the grams per unit, with standard portions of a 12 oz (355 ml) beer, a 5 oz (148 ml) glass of wine and 1.5 oz (44 ml) of 80-proof (40%) spirits (Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 1st paragraph). Whether intake was measured once or repeatedly in each cohort is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Intake categories against non-drinkers (labelled none in Table 2): <2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60 and >60 g/day, which the paper equates with about <0.5, 0.5–1, 1–2.5, 2.5–5 and 5 or more drinks a day (but see reporting issues). The main contrast is any current drinking against none. The discussion defines moderate drinking, after the 2005 US dietary guidelines, as up to 1 drink (12.5 g) a day for women and 2 drinks (25 g) for men. Drinking pattern (heavy episodes) was not analysed, and the authors say few studies gave beverage-specific estimates.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through the primary studies' adjustment. Smoking was a covariate in some studies; a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies controlling for smoking, age and sex is reported in words as giving similar results (Results › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd paragraph). Other drug use is not mentioned.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (prospective cohorts; exposure measured at baseline).

comparison.controls: Non-drinkers at baseline in each cohort (current non-drinkers; in most studies this group included former drinkers). Sensitivity analyses used the subset of studies with lifetime abstainers as the reference (9, 9, 7, 7 and 3 studies for CVD mortality, incident CHD, CHD mortality, incident stroke and stroke mortality) and pooled former drinkers against non-drinkers (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Primary studies adjusted for between 0 and 18 covariates (mean 6, SD 4): 68 of 84 gave adjusted estimates, 8 only unadjusted estimates and 8 adjustment for basic demographics only (Results › Study quality). The covariates of each study are in appendix tables 1–5 (not read).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review did not assess which confounders each study measured; it counted covariates. Health before baseline, reasons for not drinking, socio-economic position, diet and physical activity are not examined at review level (the discussion asserts that smoking, diet and exercise were controlled in the primary studies). Changes in drinking over follow-up are discussed as possible misclassification but not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; how the non-drinker groups differed from drinkers in smoking or other substance use is not described at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Cardiovascular events as ascertained by each cohort (ascertainment methods not reported at review level): CVD mortality (fatal cardiovascular or stroke events); incident CHD (fatal or non-fatal incident myocardial infarction, angina, ischaemic heart disease or coronary revascularisation); CHD mortality (fatal myocardial infarction or ischaemic heart disease); incident stroke (ischaemic or haemorrhagic); stroke mortality; all-cause mortality as a secondary outcome (Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was represented by two features only, duration of follow-up and the number of covariates in each study's model (after Egger et al. and Laupacis et al.); no risk-of-bias tool was applied (Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk as the common measure: hazard ratios and incidence density ratios taken as relative risks; odds ratios converted to relative risks with the Zhang–Yu formula (four studies; sensitivity analysis excluding them). Where a study reported only intake-specific estimates, these were first pooled within the study by random effects into a single drinkers-against-non-drinkers estimate (Methods › Data synthesis and analysis, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). Incident CHD includes angina, although studies of stable angina were excluded as ineligible.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six outcomes (five primary, all-cause mortality secondary); Table 2 alone holds 74 pooled estimates across the five primary outcomes (editors' count), and the text adds two stroke-subtype and three all-cause estimates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers (SEB, PER) independently screened all abstracts (kappa 0.86, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.91), reviewed full texts and extracted data, resolving disagreements by consensus (Methods › Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data extraction and quality assessment, 3rd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooled relative risks with 95% CIs (Stata metan); Cochran's Q (P≤0.10) and I² for heterogeneity; funnel plots and Begg's rank-correlation test for publication bias; cumulative meta-analysis. All against non-drinkers (mostly current non-drinkers) unless stated. Most-adjusted estimates: CVD mortality 0.75 (0.70 to 0.80), 21 studies, 1,184,956 participants; incident CHD 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77), 29 studies, 549,504; CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81), 31 studies, 1,925,106; incident stroke 0.98 (0.91 to 1.06), 17 studies, 458,811; stroke mortality 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23), 10 studies, 723,571. Against lifetime abstainers: 0.82 (0.78 to 0.86), 0.73 (0.61 to 0.88), 0.75 (0.66 to 0.85), 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02) and 1.29 (1.09 to 1.53) respectively. Former drinkers against non-drinkers: 1.48 (1.23 to 1.79), 1.10 (0.91 to 1.33), 1.31 (1.02 to 1.68), 0.87 (0.72 to 1.07), stroke mortality not reported. All-cause mortality (31 studies): 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); at 2.5–14.9 g/day 0.83 (0.80 to 0.86); above 60 g/day 1.30 (1.22 to 1.38). Intake-category, sex, adjustment and follow-up strata are in the key findings. Heterogeneity is quantified once (I² 72.2%, P<0.001, for the analyses in Figures 2–4); no tau², prediction intervals or absolute risks are given.
analysis.covariates: None at review level: each study's most-adjusted estimate was pooled, which for 8 studies was unadjusted and for 8 adjusted for demographics only. The examinations of confounding are a median split by number of covariates (cut points 5 to 7) and a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies adjusting for smoking, age and sex (no numbers given). The least-adjusted and most-adjusted pools contain different numbers of studies (for example 10 against 31 for CHD mortality), so their similarity does not show the effect of adjustment within the same studies.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods say a predetermined protocol was followed and the contributors' statement says all authors developed it, but it was not registered, published or cited and its content is not described; reporting followed MOOSE (Methods › Data sources and searches, 1st paragraph; Contributors).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the most-adjusted any-drinking estimates and the intake of lowest risk, but not the lifetime-abstainer analysis in which stroke mortality was higher in drinkers (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53), nor the higher CVD and CHD mortality of former drinkers. I² is given for one analysis only. The sensitivity analyses excluding converted odds ratios and restricted to studies adjusted for smoking, age and sex are described only in words.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Several stratified estimates rest on 3 or 4 studies (stroke mortality against lifetime abstainers, 3; women's stroke mortality, 3; incident stroke at >60 g/day, 4; several intake categories for stroke, 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In prospective cohorts, people who drank at baseline had a lower pooled risk of CVD death, incident CHD and CHD death than non-drinkers (RR 0.71 to 0.75, that is 25 to 29% lower; editors' arithmetic), and no different risk of incident stroke (0.98) or stroke death (1.06). The lower CHD risk was similar at every intake from 2.5 g/day to more than 60 g/day (0.66 to 0.79), was also seen in the 7 to 9 studies that used lifetime abstainers (0.73 to 0.82), and was similar in men and women. Against lifetime abstainers, stroke death was higher in drinkers (1.29, 3 studies). Former drinkers had higher CVD and CHD mortality than non-drinkers (1.48; 1.31). More than 60 g/day was associated with higher incident stroke (1.62) and higher all-cause mortality (1.30); the lowest all-cause mortality was at 2.5–14.9 g/day (0.83), in the 31 cardiovascular studies that also reported deaths from all causes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion uses association language, but the article goes further. (1) The summary box says the results "confirm the beneficial effects of moderate alcohol consumption" (What this study adds), and the discussion calls the association beyond question and builds an argument for causation on Hill's criteria (Discussion › An argument for causation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Its dose–response criterion, a greater protective association with increasing dose, is contradicted by its own Table 2 and results text (CHD risk flat above 2.5 g/day; U- or J-shaped relations for CVD mortality and stroke), and its statement that only a very strong unmeasured confounder could explain the association rests on no bias analysis. (2) The abstract calls the pooled estimates adjusted, although 8 studies contributed only unadjusted estimates. (3) The abstract says CHD mortality was lowest at 1–2 drinks a day; Table 2 shows similar estimates from 2.5 g/day upwards, with the lowest point estimate above 60 g/day. (4) The results text says that restricting to lifetime abstainers changed nothing substantive, while Table 2 shows stroke mortality moving from 1.06 to 1.29 (1.09 to 1.53). (5) The implications propose counselling selected patients to add moderate drinking to their diet and public messages of net benefit, partly on an all-cause analysis that was a by-product of the cardiovascular search (Discussion › Implications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs). (6) The discussion presents the 2.5–14.9 g/day estimates as reductions compared with abstaining, while the comparator was mostly current non-drinkers including former drinkers. In the paper's favour, the discussion states that observational studies cannot establish causation and asks for trials before any clinical use.

timeline.event: Corrao et al. (Addiction) meta-analysis reported a J-shaped relation between alcohol and CHD, against the L shape described by Maclure (1993); this review sides with the L shape for CHD (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
Fillmore et al. (Addiction Research & Theory) on systematic error in prospective studies of moderate drinking and mortality: listed by this review among earlier reviews (ref. 5) but not discussed.
Companion review by the same authors of interventional studies of alcohol and biomarkers of CHD risk (Brien et al., BMJ 2011;342:d636), on which this review's causal argument relies; not read.
This review: drinkers against mostly current non-drinkers, RR about 0.75 for CVD and CHD outcomes, no association with stroke.

Roerecke & Rehm (Addiction) criticize this review for comparing drinkers with current non-drinkers, so ignoring former drinkers, and for not reporting intake-specific risks by sex against lifetime abstainers; in their analysis restricted to sex- and end point-stratified studies against lifetime abstainers, men's IHD mortality was not significantly lower at about 1 or 2 drinks a day (read in this round; card sc_roerecke_2012).

Roerecke & Rehm (BMC Medicine) cite this review's estimates above 60 g/day (incident CHD 0.76, 0.52 to 1.09; CHD mortality 0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) as an apparent benefit of heavy drinking that appears only with current non-drinkers as the reference; their own 2014 meta-analysis against lifetime abstainers found IHD mortality of 1.00 (0.74 to 1.36) in men drinking 60 g/day or more (read in this round; card sc_roerecke_2014).

Holmes et al. (BMJ) Mendelian randomization analysis of an ADH1B variant (rs1229984) associated with lower drinking: as summarized by Roerecke & Rehm (2014), its authors concluded that higher average consumption increased IHD risk at every level of drinking, that is, no protective effect. It is on the Tier A list with the later genetic analyses of Millwood et al. (2019), Biddinger et al. (2022) and Larsson et al. (2020), read in this round by another reader.
Mukamal, Stampfer & Rimm (European Journal of Epidemiology), listed on the Tier A list as a critique of the Mendelian randomization studies; Mukamal is a co-author of this review. Not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled observational association between current drinking and lower CHD risk relative to non-drinkers was similar in earlier meta-analyses (by the authors' account) and in Roerecke & Rehm's (2012) all-studies analysis against lifetime abstainers. What is contested is whether it is causal: the reference group in most cohorts includes former drinkers, the sex- and end point-stratified analysis against lifetime abstainers weakens it at 1 to 2 drinks a day, and Mendelian randomization studies point the other way. The review's numbers should be cited with their comparator (mostly current non-drinkers), with the note that 8 of its studies contributed unadjusted estimates, and without the authors' causal reading.

funding.funder: Contracted operating grant from the Program of Research Integrating Substance Use Information into Mainstream Healthcare (PRISM), funded by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (project No 58529), with cofunding printed as by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services and the Administration Center for Substance Abuse Treatment. Personal awards: a Frederick Banting and Charles Best Canada Graduate Scholarship from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (PER); a Postdoctoral Fellowship Award from the Alberta Heritage Foundation for Medical Research (SEB); a Canada Research Chair in Health Services Research and a Senior Health Scholar Award from the Alberta Heritage Foundation for Medical Research (WAG). The paper states that the study was conducted independently of the funders and that none had an active role in preparing, reviewing or editing the manuscript (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: ICMJE forms completed. The authors declare the support above for the submitted work, no financial relationships in the previous three years with any organisation that might have an interest in the submitted work, and no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced it (Competing interests). No alcohol-industry funding or ties are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Calgary (Community Health Sciences; Medicine), the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, and Harvard Medical School and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (K J Mukamal). Mukamal is an author of four included cohort reports (Mukamal 2003, 2005 and 2006; Tolstrup 2006; refs 77–79 and 94), so review authors extracted data from their own studies; no procedure for this is described. The causal argument leans on the authors' own companion review.

what_would_settle_it: A long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking against abstention with cardiovascular events as the outcome would settle causation. Short of that: an individual-participant re-analysis of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories that separates lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, with repeated intake measures and pre-baseline health status, set beside genetic analyses able to test the shape of the curve at low intake.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adults without cardiovascular disease), exposure (current drinking), comparator (non-drinkers), five outcomes and the prospective cohort design are specified (Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

A predetermined protocol is mentioned, but it was not registered, published or cited, its content is not described and no deviations are discussed (as on other project cards, an unregistered, undescribed protocol is judged no).

Only prospective cohorts were included; the introduction explains that no clinical trials exist. The exclusion of case-control designs is not explained, but the item concerns the choice between randomized and non-randomized designs.

Medline and Embase with the search themes given, no language restriction, published and unpublished studies eligible, bibliographies, conference proceedings (2007–2009) and expert contact, with the search ending about 15 months before acceptance. No study registry was searched, which the item requires for a full yes.
Two reviewers independently screened all abstracts (kappa 0.86) and reviewed full texts, resolving disagreements by consensus.
Both reviewers independently extracted data from all included studies, with consensus on disagreements.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusion categories are described in the text (ineligible outcomes, non-atherothrombotic or composite end points, non-cardiovascular outcomes, duplicates) and Figure 1 (an image) shows the flow, but no list of the 47 studies excluded at full text with reasons is given; by the text's account the appendix holds adjustment tables and cumulative plots (not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives cohort, size, country, percentage of men, age range, follow-up and outcomes; exposure categories, reference group and covariates by study are only in appendix tables (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool: quality was reduced to length of follow-up and the number of covariates in each model. A covariate count does not show whether the important confounders were controlled, and selection bias (how the non-drinker group was formed, health-related selection at baseline) was not appraised study by study; the lifetime-abstainer subset analysis addresses one form of it only at the synthesis level. A lenient reading could give partial yes; the overall rating is the same either way.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling is appropriate in itself, but the most-adjusted pools combine adjusted estimates with the unadjusted estimates of 8 studies without a stated reason; where a study reported only intake-specific estimates, these were pooled within the study by random effects as if independent, although they share one reference group, which overstates the precision of that study's estimate; and intake categories were pooled separately without dose–response modelling.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Analyses stratified by number of covariates and length of follow-up, a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies adjusting for smoking, age and sex, and the lifetime-abstainer subset examine how these features affect the pooled estimates, although with crude quality markers (Table 2; Results › Sensitivity analyses).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations mention variable follow-up and adjustment, but the conclusions do not take risk of bias into account: the discussion argues for causation, treats confounding as excluded because estimates were similar across adjustment strata, and addresses former drinkers in the reference group only to say they did not seem to bias the results.

Heterogeneity was tested (one I² reported, 72.2%), investigated through stratified and sensitivity analyses and discussed (attributed to the large samples). I² is not reported per outcome and no tau² or prediction interval is given.

Funnel plots and Begg's test for each outcome (P from 0.089 to 0.75), with the conclusion that publication bias was unlikely; Begg's test has low power and the funnel plots are images that were not checked.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and competing interests are reported for the review.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2, protocol; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk-of-bias assessment; 11, statistical methods; 13, interpretation), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; items 2 and 7 alone would keep it critically low under the most lenient reading of the others. The review has real strengths: duplicate screening and extraction, a search without language limits that admitted unpublished studies, and sensitivity analyses that report the lifetime-abstainer and former-drinker contrasts. Its pooled numbers can be cited as a description of what cohorts published to 2009 reported for drinkers against mostly current non-drinkers, each with its comparator; they cannot be cited as effects of drinking, and the review's causal reading is the authors' argument, not a result.

key_findings.finding: Search to September 2009 (Medline from 1950, Embase from 1980), without language restriction and with unpublished studies eligible: 4235 unique citations, 131 potentially relevant studies, 84 included prospective cohort publications; 34 (40%) studied all-male cohorts, 6 (7%) women only and 44 (52%) both sexes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Data sources and searches, 1st paragraph; Results › Identification of studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: People who drank at baseline against non-drinkers (mostly current non-drinkers, a group that in most studies included former drinkers), pooled most-adjusted relative risks: CVD mortality 0.75 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.80), 21 studies, 1,184,956 participants; incident CHD 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77), 29 studies, 549,504; CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81), 31 studies, 1,925,106; incident stroke 0.98 (0.91 to 1.06), 17 studies, 458,811; stroke mortality 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23), 10 studies, 723,571.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (column headers; row Most adjusted models); Abstract, Results
key_findings.note: Most adjusted means each study's most-adjusted estimate: 8 of the 84 studies reported only unadjusted estimates and 8 adjusted only for demographic variables (Results › Study quality), so not all of these are adjusted estimates, as the abstract implies. Participant totals may count some people twice (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Least-adjusted pooled estimates, drinkers against non-drinkers, from fewer studies: CVD mortality 0.84 (0.75 to 0.95), 11 studies; incident CHD 0.73 (0.65 to 0.82), 14; CHD mortality 0.80 (0.70 to 0.91), 10; incident stroke 1.01 (0.88 to 1.16), 10; stroke mortality 1.13 (0.96 to 1.32), 3. The authors describe least- and most-adjusted estimates as generally similar.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (row Least adjusted models); Results › Primary analyses of cardiovascular disease mortality, coronary heart disease incidence and mortality, and stroke incidence and mortality, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The two rows pool different sets of studies, so the comparison does not show the effect of adjustment within the same studies.

key_findings.finding: With lifetime abstainers as the reference (subset of studies): CVD mortality 0.82 (0.78 to 0.86), 9 studies; incident CHD 0.73 (0.61 to 0.88), 9; CHD mortality 0.75 (0.66 to 0.85), 7; incident stroke 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02), 7; stroke mortality 1.29 (1.09 to 1.53), 3 studies, that is, higher in drinkers than in lifetime abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (row Active drinkers v lifetime abstainers); Results › Sensitivity analyses, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text says the estimates did not change substantively with this reference group; for stroke mortality they did (1.06 to 1.29), on 3 studies. Not in the abstract.

key_findings.finding: Former drinkers against non-drinkers: CVD mortality 1.48 (1.23 to 1.79), 6 studies; CHD mortality 1.31 (1.02 to 1.68), 6; incident CHD 1.10 (0.91 to 1.33), 8; incident stroke 0.87 (0.72 to 1.07), 4; stroke mortality not reported (2 studies). The authors conclude that former drinkers had higher cardiovascular and coronary death rates but not more incident events, and that including former drinkers in the reference group did not seem to bias the results.

key_findings.note: The table labels the comparison former drinkers against non-drinkers; the text describes it as former drinkers against drinkers (see reporting issues).

CHD mortality: 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), 6; 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), 18; 0.79 (0.71 to 0.88), 15; 0.77 (0.72 to 0.83), 12; 0.75 (0.63 to 0.89), 9. The authors describe similar risk reduction at all intakes above 2.5 g/day, an L-shaped relation for CHD.

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality (secondary analysis of the 31 included studies that reported it), drinkers against non-drinkers: 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); J-shaped, lowest at 2.5–14.9 g/day (0.83, 0.80 to 0.86; 16 studies) and higher above 60 g/day (1.30, 1.22 to 1.38; 8 studies).
key_findings.locator: Results › Mortality from all causes, 1st paragraph; Abstract, Results
key_findings.note: The studies were found by a search for cardiovascular outcomes, not for all-cause mortality; the comparator is mostly current non-drinkers.

key_findings.finding: Study quality markers: follow-up 2.5 to 35 years (mean 11, SD 6), 13 studies (15%) with 5 years or less; 0 to 18 covariates (mean 6, SD 4); 68 studies gave adjusted estimates, 8 only unadjusted estimates and 8 adjustment for basic demographics only.

Heterogeneity: the forest plots for CVD mortality, incident CHD and CHD mortality (Figures 2–4) are described as showing little visual heterogeneity despite statistical heterogeneity (P<0.001, I² 72.2%), which the authors attribute to more than one million participants; all study point estimates except one (CVD mortality) and two (CHD) are said to lie below 1.0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary analyses of cardiovascular disease mortality, coronary heart disease incidence and mortality, and stroke incidence and mortality, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: One I² is given for three outcomes without saying which; the forest plots are images and were not checked.

key_findings.finding: Publication bias: funnel plots judged symmetrical; Begg's test P = 0.40 (CVD mortality), 0.75 (incident CHD), 0.089 (CHD mortality), 0.33 (incident stroke), 0.59 (stroke mortality) and 0.26 (all-cause mortality).

Sensitivity analyses excluding the four studies whose odds ratios were converted to relative risks, and restricted to studies adjusting for smoking, age and sex, are reported only in words as making little difference. Cumulative meta-analysis showed little change in the CVD mortality and incident CHD estimates with studies added after 1999, and for CHD mortality from 1992–3 (appendix figures, not read).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data synthesis and analysis, 3rd paragraph; Results › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure units: intake in grams of ethanol per day, with 12.5 g per drink where a study did not report grams and standard portions of 355 ml beer, 148 ml wine and 44 ml of 40% spirits; categories <2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60 and >60 g/day. The discussion's definition of moderate drinking is up to 12.5 g (one drink) a day for women and 25 g (two drinks) for men, after the 2005 US dietary guidelines.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 1st paragraph; Discussion › An argument for causation, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the lowest risk of CHD mortality occurred at 1–2 drinks a day, but Table 2 gives CHD mortality estimates of 0.79, 0.79, 0.77 and 0.75 for 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60 and >60 g/day, so the lowest point estimate is in the heaviest category; the results text describes similar reductions at all intakes above 2.5 g/day and the discussion an L shape.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Table 2; Results › Analyses of dose response, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's dose statement for CHD mortality is not supported by the paper's own table; claims about the intake of lowest CHD risk must use Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says that restricting to studies with lifetime abstainers as the reference did not change the estimates substantively, but Table 2 shows stroke mortality at 1.29 (1.09 to 1.53) against lifetime abstainers (3 studies), compared with 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23) against all non-drinkers; CVD mortality also moves from 0.75 to 0.82.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Sensitivity analyses, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The one significant adverse association in the main analyses is described as no change; claims about the reference-group sensitivity analysis must quote the table, outcome by outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 labels the former-drinker row as former drinkers against non-drinkers, while the text says the risk of CVD and CHD death was significantly higher in former drinkers than in drinkers.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 (row Former drinkers v non-drinkers); Results › Sensitivity analyses, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparator of the former-drinker estimates (1.48 and 1.31) is ambiguous; the table's label (non-drinkers, presumably those who never drank) should be used, with the ambiguity noted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the headline estimates pooled adjusted relative risks, but they are each study's most-adjusted estimate, which for 8 studies was unadjusted and for another 8 adjusted only for demographics.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Results › Study quality, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline estimates mix adjusted and crude associations; they should not be described as adjusted without qualification.

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity is quantified once (I² 72.2%, P<0.001) for the analyses shown in Figures 2–4 together, without saying which outcome it belongs to; no I² is reported for the stroke, all-cause or stratified analyses.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Primary analyses of cardiovascular disease mortality, coronary heart disease incidence and mortality, and stroke incidence and mortality, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The consistency of the pooled estimates cannot be judged outcome by outcome from the text; the forest plots (images) were not checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The implications cite the secondary analysis of overall mortality as fig 5, but Figure 5 is the forest plot of incident stroke; all-cause mortality is Figure 7.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Implications, 3rd paragraph; Figures 5 and 7 (legends)
reporting_issues.consequence: Figure cross-reference error; no effect on the numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Two Table 1 entries do not fit the stated inclusion criteria: Burke et al. (2007) has an age range of 15–88 years against the criterion of adults aged 18 or over, and Hammar et al. (1997) is titled in the reference list as a case-referent study, against the criterion of prospective cohort design.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (Burke 2007 and Hammar 1997 rows); references 29 and 53
reporting_issues.consequence: The criteria were not applied strictly, or the table and titles misdescribe these studies; each contributes to the incident CHD pool.

reporting_issues.issue: With the stated 12.5 g per drink, the category <2.5 g/day is less than 0.2 drink and 2.5–14.9 g/day is about 0.2 to 1.2 drinks (editors' arithmetic), but the Methods label them as <0.5 drink and about 0.5–1 drink.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The drink-equivalent labels of the lowest categories are inexact; claims should give the categories in grams per day.

reporting_issues.issue: Some pooled participant counts may include the same people twice or overstate the analysed samples: Garg et al. (Table 1: 1992; reference list: 1993) and Rehm et al. (1997) are both listed as National Health and Nutrition Examination Study cohorts contributing to CHD mortality, and Solomon et al. (2000), whose title describes a study confined to women with type 2 diabetes, is listed with 121,700 Nurses' Health Study participants, more than the whole-cohort Nurses' Health Study analyses in the same table (Chiuve 2008, 71,243; Fuchs 1995, 85,709), so the figure is probably the parent cohort rather than the women analysed (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Garg, Rehm and Solomon rows); Table 2 (column headers); references 47, 83 and 90
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant totals in Table 2 (for example 1,925,106 for CHD mortality) and the claim of more than one million participants should be cited as the authors' sums, not as counts of distinct people; whether overlapping cohorts entered the same pool is not addressed.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: the text says the women's stroke estimates rest on only three pooled studies, while Table 2 gives 4 studies for women's incident stroke and 3 for stroke mortality; Table 1 spells the Busselton cohort as Brusselton and dates Garg et al. 1992 against 1993 in the reference list.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Table 2 (rows Sex); reference 47
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the pooled estimates.
